hero.headline: Trump announces economic campaign against Iran, threatens China sanctions
hero.body:
Trump Extends Iran Ceasefire While Threatening Economic Pressure

President Trump announced an extension of a ceasefire with Iran on Tuesday, pausing military action while demanding Iranian leaders submit a unified peace proposal. The announcement came after weeks of escalating tensions and failed diplomatic efforts between the two nations.

Trump stated on his Truth Social platform that he was extending the ceasefire "until such time as their leaders and representatives can come up with a unified proposal." He credited requests from Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and other officials in his decision to delay military strikes. However, Trump emphasized that the U.S. military would "remain ready and able" and that the blockade on Iranian ports would continue.

The decision marked a sharp reversal from Trump's earlier statements. Hours before announcing the extension, Trump said he "expected to be bombing" and that the military was "raring to go." The administration has threatened to target Iranian power stations and civilian infrastructure in any renewed attacks.

Iran's response has been dismissive. Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, speaker of the Iranian parliament and the regime's lead negotiator, rejected the ceasefire extension. His adviser, Mahdi Mohammadi, wrote on social media that Trump's move was "a ploy to buy time for a surprise strike" and that "the time for Iran to take the initiative has come."

The dispute centers on several key issues. Iran has insisted the U.S. must end its blockade of Iranian ports before negotiations can resume. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that the blockade would continue, stating that within days Iranian oil storage facilities would be full and Iranian wells would shut down.

Trump has also announced plans for what he calls "economic D-Day" against Iran, declaring it "the most crushing economic operation ever taken against any country." Bessent has promised to announce "the toughest sanctions in history" against Iran. The administration has threatened to target any country, business, or banking institution that supports Iran economically.

The ongoing conflict has disrupted global energy markets. Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, a critical shipping lane through which about a fifth of the world's oil and gas passes. The International Energy Agency called the combined effects of this conflict and Russia's war with Ukraine "the biggest crisis in history" for global energy markets. Oil prices have risen above ninety dollars per barrel as a result.

Pakistan has emerged as a key mediator in the dispute. Prime Minister Sharif thanked Trump for the ceasefire extension and pledged to continue efforts toward "a negotiated settlement of the conflict."

The first round of talks in Islamabad ten days earlier ended without agreement on reopening the strait or other key issues. Iran's foreign minister has rejected U.S. threats, calling them "desperate" and insisting that Iran will not negotiate "under the shadow of threats."

cards.headline: U.S. Marines Cancel Joint Military Drill With South Korea, Citing Iran War Demands
cards.body:
The United States Marine Corps has called off a major joint military exercise with South Korea, citing operational demands related to the ongoing conflict with Iran. South Korea announced that the decision to cancel the high-profile event was communicated in June. The cancellation marks another reduction in U.S. military cooperation with its key East Asian ally.

The canceled drill was considered a significant component of the military partnership between Washington and Seoul, designed to maintain readiness and demonstrate alliance cohesion in the region. President Trump had already shortened another joint military exercise with South Korea earlier this month, reflecting broader shifts in U.S. defense priorities as resources are redirected to the Middle East.

The decision comes as U.S. forces face increasing demands in the Iran theater. The reallocation of military assets and personnel to address the conflict appears to be affecting long-standing security commitments in other regions. South Korean officials confirmed receiving notification of the cancellation two months ago, though details about alternative arrangements or future exercises were not provided.

The cancellation could have implications for regional security dynamics in East Asia, where joint U.S.-South Korea military exercises have traditionally served as a deterrent and a signal of American commitment to defending its ally. The exercises have historically been viewed as essential to maintaining combat readiness and interoperability between the two nations' armed forces.

The move reflects the strategic trade-offs the United States faces as it manages multiple international commitments simultaneously. With military resources stretched between existing alliance obligations and active conflict zones, decisions about where to deploy forces and conduct exercises carry significant diplomatic and security ramifications for partners across different regions.

cards.headline: Syrian and Israeli Officials Hold U.S.-Mediated Talks to Reduce Tensions
cards.teaser: The discussions came after Israel struck an air base in northwestern Syria in its latest military intervention.
cards.body:
Syria and Israel held talks mediated by the United States to reduce tensions between the two countries, according to Syrian state media. The discussions occurred days after Israel struck an air base in northwestern Syria.

The Israeli strike represents the latest in a series of military operations Israel has conducted on Syrian territory. The U.S.-mediated dialogue reflects diplomatic efforts to manage escalating friction in the region.

cards.headline: Nearly 90,000 ordered to evacuate as wildfire nears Reno, Nevada
cards.body:
A rapidly spreading wildfire in Nevada has forced nearly 90,000 residents to leave their homes as flames advance toward Reno. The fire, named the Hawk fire, has burned more than 15,000 acres and remains completely uncontained as of Sunday.

The evacuation zone has expanded to the edge of the University of Nevada campus as strong winds, low humidity, and dry vegetation accelerate the blaze's spread. Of those ordered to evacuate, 42,000 are under strict evacuation orders while an additional 45,000 are in the evacuation warning zone and encouraged to leave immediately.

"If you have been told to evacuate, please don't wait!" Reno Mayor Hillary Schieve said in a statement on social media. "Structures have already been burned in this fire and your life is more important than a building. Evacuating before the fire arrives also allows our firefighters to focus their efforts on battling the blaze."

The fire was human-caused, though authorities have not released details about how it started as investigations continue. Three civilians and three first responders have been injured, and several structures have been destroyed.

Governor Joe Lombardo declared a state of emergency in Washoe County and mobilized the Nevada National Guard to support response efforts. Two helicopter crews have been deployed for aerial firefighting operations, while 60 troops have been assigned to protect evacuated neighborhoods. Around 400 personnel from local, state, and federal agencies are working on the incident, including ground crews and air resources.

The fire's rapid growth has challenged firefighting efforts. Washoe County Sheriff Darin Balaam described how changing wind patterns sent flames in different directions, making conditions "extremely confusing." On Saturday night, the fire moved exceptionally fast, jumping over fire trucks and complicating efforts for responders to reach hotspots while residents evacuated.

The expanding fire has caused widespread disruption. Nearly 10,000 homes and businesses in Washoe County lost power on Sunday. At least 20 road closures were in effect, including portions of US Route 395, a major north-south highway. The Reno-Stead airport closed to general aviation but remained open to firefighting aircraft. The University of Nevada's Reno campus remained just outside the evacuation zone with an enrollment of about 24,000 students.

Emergency officials opened the Reno-Sparks Convention Center to evacuees, though pets were not permitted there. Small and large animals were directed to two separate locations. Casinos in Reno offered discounted hotel rooms to those evacuated.

Authorities also monitored a county detention facility located several blocks from the evacuation warning zone's outer edge, with plans in place for potential evacuation if conditions worsen. The Hawk fire follows three other wildfires that forced more than 13,000 residents to evacuate earlier in August.

cards.headline: US and Canadian businesses brace for impact as tariff dispute escalates
cards.teaser: Companies on both sides of the border express concern about loss of revenue as retaliatory trade measures continue.
cards.body:
'Half my business will be gone' - Firms in Canada and US fear trade war

The US has imposed 50% tariffs on roughly $20 billion of Canadian goods, including items ranging from hockey sticks to tongue depressors. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has pledged to respond with matching tariffs "dollar for dollar" following the collapse of trade negotiations.

Trade experts say the escalating dispute could result in job losses, though the largest impact is expected to be political, further straining the relationship between the two traditional allies. Business owners on both sides of the border face significant challenges as integrated North American supply chains and cross-border operations face mounting uncertainty.

cards.headline: Russia Warns UK as New Prime Minister Burnham Makes First Foreign Trip to Ukraine
cards.teaser: Prime Minister Andy Burnham traveled to Kyiv in his first foreign visit since taking office as Moscow issued new warnings.
cards.body:
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham is visiting Kyiv, drawing a comparison between Ukraine's war against Russia and Britain's fight against Nazi Germany. During the trip, the UK plans to share blueprints for long-range missiles with Ukraine.

The Kremlin has responded with sharp criticism, with spokesman Peskov accusing Britain of "methodically and regularly throwing oil on the fire" and plotting to prevent peace progress. Moscow warned that sharing missile technology would "add fuel to fire" in British-Russian relations.

cards.headline: Russian Drone Guided Entirely by Artificial Intelligence Kills Three in Ukraine
cards.teaser: Ukrainian officials said the drone operated autonomously without human control during the attack.
cards.body:
A Russian drone killed three Ukrainians in an attack that Ukrainian officials said was guided entirely by artificial intelligence. The drone reportedly used an Nvidia chip and operated without direct human control during the strike.

The incident marks what Ukrainian authorities described as an escalation in autonomous weaponry on the battlefield. The use of fully AI-controlled drones raises new questions about warfare conducted by machines operating independently of human decision-making.

cards.headline: Ukrainian Strikes Hit Warehouses of Russia's Second-Largest Online Retailer
cards.teaser: Ozon reported that its warehouses across southern Russia were struck in overnight attacks.
cards.body:
Ukrainian forces struck warehouses belonging to Ozon, Russia's second-largest online retailer, in overnight attacks across southern Russia. The company confirmed that facilities in Dagestan and Krasnodar were among those hit.

These strikes represent a shift in Ukrainian targeting toward commercial infrastructure deep within Russian territory. Ozon's warehouses serve as major distribution hubs for online commerce across the affected regions.

cards.teaser: The discussions came after Israel struck an air base in northwestern Syria in its latest military intervention.

cards.headline: Landfill Collapse in Guinea Kills 31 as Rubbish Mound Buries Homes
cards.teaser: A mound of waste at a major site in the capital collapsed onto residential buildings.
cards.body:
A landslide at a massive waste dump in Conakry, Guinea's capital, killed 30 people after heavy rains caused the mound to collapse. The debris engulfed nearby tents and shacks where residents lived.

The disaster came less than a week after the government announced plans to close the site and relocate the waste due to safety concerns. The rainy season regularly triggers landslides and flash floods across West African cities, making overcrowded waste dumps particularly dangerous in areas with limited infrastructure.

cards.headline: Access to Zambian Courts Blocked as Election Petition Deadline Approaches
cards.teaser: Preparations for President Hichilema's second inauguration continue as legal challenges face barriers.
cards.body:
Access to Zambian courts has been prevented as the deadline looms for filing election petitions. Preparations for President Hakainde Hichilema's second inauguration appear to be moving forward despite the legal access issues.

The blocking of court access comes at a sensitive moment in Zambia's political calendar, when opposition parties or candidates would typically have the opportunity to challenge election results through legal channels. The timing has raised questions about the ability of potential challengers to pursue formal complaints before the inauguration proceeds.

cards.headline: National Guard members share concerns about extended Washington deployment
cards.teaser: Three National Guard members who served on the Washington deployment mission spoke about their experiences as the operation enters its second year.
cards.body:
As President Trump's National Guard deployment to Washington, D.C. enters its second year, three service members who served extended periods on the mission spoke with NPR about their experiences. One guard member expressed embarrassment about participating in the operation.

The three service members shared their reactions to the prolonged deployment, offering perspectives on what it has meant to serve an extended mission in the nation's capital during this period.

cards.headline: Former deputy convicted in Sonya Massey shooting dies in prison
cards.teaser: Sean Grayson, serving a 20-year sentence for fatally shooting Sonya Massey in her home, died while in custody.
cards.body:
Sean Grayson, a former Illinois sheriff's deputy, died Sunday while serving a 20-year prison sentence for the fatal shooting of Sonya Massey. The killing, which occurred inside Massey's home, sparked significant national debate about police use of force.

Grayson's conviction and death mark the conclusion of a case that drew widespread attention to accountability in law enforcement. His lawyer confirmed his death in prison.

cards.headline: Businesses on both sides of border brace for trade war impact
cards.teaser: Business owners in Canada and the United States face mounting uncertainty as import taxes escalate between the two countries.
cards.body:
Business owners in Canada and the United States are navigating growing uncertainty as trade tensions between the two countries intensify. One business owner stated that half their business could disappear as a result of the escalating tariffs.

The tit-for-tat import taxes have created worry among companies that depend on cross-border trade. Business owners on both sides are attempting to plan for potential disruptions as the trade dispute continues to develop.

cards.headline: IndyCar holds inaugural race on National Mall in Washington
cards.teaser: IndyCar drivers competed past major national landmarks in the first race held on the National Mall this weekend.
cards.body:
Washington, D.C. hosted its first IndyCar race this weekend on the National Mall, with drivers navigating a unique route past some of the nation's most famous landmarks. The unconventional course presented novel challenges for the professional racers.

Kyle Kirkwood won the Freedom 250 race, with President Trump officiating the start by waving the green flag to begin the event.

cards.headline: UK defense minister calls for removal of dangerous driving videos
cards.teaser: Defence minister Luke Pollard says social media platforms should remove videos showing people driving the wrong way down roads.
cards.body:
Defence minister Luke Pollard has called on social media companies to remove videos showing dangerous driving, including a trend of people driving the wrong way down roads. Pollard said there is no place for such content on social media platforms.

The minister's comments reflect concerns about viral trends that could encourage risky behavior on the roads. Authorities are working to address the issue as these videos spread online.

cards.headline: Television contestant Jo Gardiner dies at 61
cards.teaser: Jo Gardiner, who appeared on Race Across the World, has died of cancer one year after her son died in a crash.
cards.body:
Jo Gardiner, a former contestant on the television program Race Across the World, died of cancer at age 61. Her death came one year after her son died in a crash.

Gardiner had appeared on the reality travel show, which follows contestants as they race across different parts of the world. She faced the loss of her son before her own death from cancer.

hero.teaser: Companies on both sides of the border express concern about loss of revenue as retaliatory trade measures continue.

cards.headline: Shein targets $27 billion valuation for Hong Kong stock market listing
cards.teaser: The fast-fashion retailer plans to begin trading on September 1 in one of the year's largest public offerings.
cards.body:
Fast-fashion retailer Shein will list on the Hong Kong stock exchange on September 1 at a valuation of nearly $27 billion. The valuation represents a significant decline from the company's $100 billion private market peak four years ago.

The listing comes as Shein faces mounting challenges. The China-based online retailer swung to a $99 million loss in the first quarter of this year. The company has also drawn scrutiny over its environmental footprint as it continues its rapid expansion in the fast-fashion sector.

cards.headline: Federal probe of Dodgers owner's insurance empire rattles industry
cards.teaser: Investigations into Mark Walter's business operations highlight risks in private-equity-owned insurance companies.
cards.body:
Federal investigations into the business empire of Los Angeles Dodgers owner Mark Walter have drawn attention to practices at private-equity-owned insurance companies. The scrutiny focuses on insurers that invest customer premiums in higher-risk assets.

The probe has created uncertainty across the insurance sector about regulatory tolerance for investment strategies employed by private-equity-backed carriers. How insurers manage premium dollars and balance investment returns against policyholder protections has become a focal point for regulators examining the industry.

cards.headline: Streaming platforms compete to become single destination for video subscriptions
cards.teaser: Netflix, YouTube, and Amazon are racing to let users subscribe to multiple services through one app.
cards.body:
Major streaming platforms are competing to become the primary hub where viewers manage all their video subscriptions. YouTube is working to match Amazon's existing capability that allows users to subscribe to services like HBO Max directly within its app. Netflix is also showing increased openness to the model.

The shift represents a strategic battle over which company will control the relationship with subscribers and collect data on viewing habits across multiple services. Whichever platform succeeds in becoming the central subscription gateway could gain significant leverage over smaller streaming competitors.

cards.headline: England and Wales review could reshape business rates for pubs and hotels
cards.teaser: A government examination of the rating system may lead to changes in how commercial property taxes are calculated.
cards.body:
Pubs and hotels in England and Wales could see changes to their business rates following a government review of the current system. The examination focuses on how rates are calculated for commercial properties.

The review has raised expectations in the hospitality industry that the tax burden on physical premises could be restructured. Business rates have been a persistent concern for pub and hotel operators who argue the current system places them at a disadvantage compared to online competitors with smaller physical footprints.

cards.headline: China recalls nearly three million Teslas over door handle safety issue
cards.teaser: Hidden door handles on electric vehicles from multiple manufacturers are being addressed in a major safety recall.
cards.body:
Chinese regulators have ordered Tesla to recall approximately 2.98 million vehicles manufactured in or imported to China, including Model 3, Model Y, Model X, and Model S models. The recall addresses safety concerns related to door handles.

The action is part of a broader regulatory push, with Chinese authorities announcing plans to ban hidden car door handles. Other carmakers including XPeng, Xiaomi, and Geely are also conducting recalls related to similar safety issues, indicating a widespread industry concern rather than a problem unique to Tesla.

cards.headline: CrossCountry restores train service after system outage
cards.teaser: The rail operator resumed operations following disruptions that affected national service over the weekend.
cards.body:
CrossCountry train services have returned to normal operation after a system outage caused widespread disruptions. The problems followed major national rail disruption over the weekend.

The restoration of service ends a period of travel difficulties for passengers using the rail network. The company has not provided details on what caused the outage or what steps have been taken to prevent similar disruptions.

hero.headline: Uber faces nearly $1 billion fine over automated driver suspensions
hero.body:
The Dutch Data Protection Authority is imposing a fine of 825 million euros on Uber for violations related to its automated driver suspension system. The penalty represents the second largest enforcement action issued under the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation.

The fine addresses concerns about how Uber processed personal data through its automated systems for suspending drivers. The Dutch authority concluded that the company's practices violated GDPR requirements, which mandate strict protections for personal data and impose limits on fully automated decision-making that significantly affects individuals.

Uber operates across Europe with a network of drivers who work through its app-based platform. The company's automated suspension system has been a point of contention, as drivers can lose access to the platform and their income through decisions made without direct human review. The GDPR requires companies to provide meaningful information about automated decision-making and give individuals the right to contest such decisions.

The 825 million euro penalty places this enforcement action behind only a previous fine issued to a major technology company. GDPR allows regulators to fine companies up to four percent of their annual global revenue for serious violations. European data protection authorities have increasingly scrutinized how companies use automated systems to make consequential decisions about individuals.

Uber has faced regulatory challenges across multiple European jurisdictions over its employment practices and data handling. The company must now address the Dutch authority's findings or potentially appeal the decision through European courts. The penalty adds to mounting pressure on technology platforms to provide greater transparency and human oversight in automated systems that affect workers and users.

cards.headline: Mystery AI model Ox Alpha sparks speculation online
cards.teaser: A new artificial intelligence model called Ox Alpha has generated intense interest and speculation in technology communities.
cards.body:
A mysterious artificial intelligence model named Ox Alpha has generated widespread speculation across technology communities online. The model's creators and origins have not been publicly identified, prompting technology enthusiasts to analyze and test it in attempts to determine who built it.

The emergence of unattributed AI models reflects the broader proliferation of machine learning tools across the industry. As AI systems continue to demonstrate unexpected behaviors, questions about developer accountability and safety preparedness have come into focus within the technology sector.

cards.headline: Authors challenge legality of AI training on copyrighted books
cards.teaser: Legal questions surround whether artificial intelligence companies can use copyrighted literary works to train their models without author permission.
cards.body:
Most published authors contributed to AI development without their knowledge or consent, as companies used copyrighted books to train language models without seeking permission or offering compensation. This practice has sparked legal disputes over intellectual property rights.

Meanwhile, some Hollywood creatives are taking paid gig work to teach AI systems their professional skills. Award-winning writers, directors, and producers earn between $12 and $200 per hour training AI models in screenwriting, production, and related tasks—work some describe as undermining their own profession.

cards.headline: Surveillance firm Flock Safety faces public backlash
cards.teaser: Flock Safety is confronting increasing public opposition over concerns about potential misuse of its surveillance technology.
cards.body:
Flock Safety is experiencing significant public criticism over its surveillance technology. The company's CEO has called for compromise as opposition to the systems grows.

The company provides automated license plate readers and surveillance tools to law enforcement agencies and communities. Critics worry that widespread deployment of these systems raises privacy concerns and could enable tracking of individuals without adequate legal safeguards.

cards.headline: China delays lunar mission to 2027 citing need for absolute success
cards.teaser: China postponed the launch of its Chang'e 7 lunar mission, stating the project does not yet meet conditions for launch.
cards.body:
China delayed a planned lunar mission until 2027, citing the need for absolute success as the reason for postponement. Officials stated that the Chang'e 7 mission does not currently meet the conditions required for launch.

The Chang'e 7 mission represents part of China's broader lunar exploration program. The delay suggests Chinese space authorities are taking additional time to ensure mission readiness rather than proceeding with the originally planned timeline.

cards.headline: Waymo develops custom chip for robotaxi operations
cards.teaser: Waymo is using a custom-designed chip to power its autonomous vehicle ambitions as the company expands its robotaxi service.
cards.body:
Waymo developed a custom chip designed specifically for its robotaxi operations. The specialized hardware represents the company's effort to optimize autonomous driving systems for its commercial deployment.

Custom chips allow autonomous vehicle companies to tailor processing power to their specific needs rather than relying on general-purpose hardware. Waymo has expanded its driverless taxi service in multiple cities as it scales up commercial operations.

cards.headline: Linkdaze launches smart calendar for household management
cards.teaser: A new digital calendar product offers household management features without requiring paid subscriptions for core functionality.
cards.body:
Linkdaze has launched a smart digital calendar designed to manage household operations beyond basic scheduling. The product includes an AI-powered meal planner and avoids putting core features behind subscription paywalls.

Smart calendars typically integrate multiple household functions like schedules, shopping lists, and meal planning into a single platform. Linkdaze's approach of offering these capabilities without requiring paid subscriptions sets it apart in the connected home market, where subscription models are common.

hero.headline: Gauff wins Cincinnati Open title ahead of US Open
hero.body:
Coco Gauff defeated Jessica Pegula 6-2, 6-4 in the Cincinnati Open final to claim her first title of 2026, arriving at the US Open with significant momentum after one of her smoothest tournament runs.

The victory holds particular significance given Gauff's struggles exactly one year earlier. At the 2025 Cincinnati Open, the American's serve had become a major liability, with double faults plaguing her matches and undermining her confidence in her overall game. That loss to Jasmine Paolini prompted a dramatic decision: Gauff hired biomechanics expert Gavin MacMillan to completely rebuild her serve from the ground up, beginning just before last year's US Open.

The timing of that overhaul was challenging. Making such a fundamental change to her technique while preparing for her most important tournament of the year drew considerable scrutiny. During her second round match at the US Open last year, Gauff cried on court as she grappled with the transformation. Over the following twelve months, she continued to struggle with double faults as she worked through the extensive biomechanical changes.

Now, Gauff has finally found confidence with her serve, and the improvement has transformed her overall performance. "I think it was a long journey, but I'm happy," she said after winning Cincinnati. "Last year I was frustrated with my game and felt like I was declining. It's not something any player wants to feel. You always want to feel like you're getting better. I made sudden decisions that most people probably wouldn't do before a slam, but I think it's worth it. It's night and day, the player I am from last year to now."

In Cincinnati, Gauff demonstrated the benefits of her serve overhaul. After dropping her first set against Liudmila Samsonova, she won ten consecutive sets to reach the final. Known for her dramatic three-set victories, Gauff deliberately sought to finish matches in straight sets this week to preserve energy before the US Open. In the final, she repeatedly hit first serves above 120 miles per hour and aggressively moved forward when opportunities presented themselves.

Her defensive excellence also proved decisive against Pegula. The third seed struggled to find answers to Gauff's mobility and court coverage. "It's just so hard when you play somebody that moves the way she does," Pegula said. "She's the best mover on tour by far. The way she's able to defend out of the corners is better than anybody else."

Pegula's path to the final was noteworthy in its own right. She won three consecutive three-set matches, including a victory over defending champion Iga Swiatek, positioning herself as another in-form American heading to the US Open.

Arthur Fils captured the men's title, defeating Frances Tiafoe 6-3, 1-6, 6-0 to claim his first Masters 1000 title. The 22-year-old French player is now ranked number 11 in the world following his breakthrough victory.

cards.headline: Norris wins Dutch Grand Prix but says McLaren lacks title-winning car
cards.teaser: Lando Norris claimed his second consecutive victory of the season at the Dutch Grand Prix but expressed doubt about championship prospects.
cards.body:
Lando Norris secured his second consecutive victory at the Dutch Grand Prix, but the McLaren driver remains cautious about his team's championship prospects. Despite the back-to-back wins, Norris stated he doesn't have the car needed to fight for a world title.

Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff, however, views McLaren and Ferrari as genuine title contenders. With Mercedes' early-season dominance fading, Wolff acknowledged the championship battle could become closer among the top teams.

cards.headline: Maradona's Hand of God ball sells for $2.5 million at auction
cards.teaser: The football Diego Maradona used to score his famous Hand of God goal against England in 1986 sold at auction.
cards.body:
Diego Maradona's iconic ball from the 1986 World Cup quarter-final has sold at auction for £2.5 million. The football was used when Maradona scored his famous "Hand of God" goal against England during Argentina's victory in that match.

The goal became one of football's most memorable and controversial moments, cementing its place in sporting history.

cards.headline: Liverpool salvage draw at Newcastle with injury-time penalty
cards.teaser: Dominik Szoboszlai converted an injury-time penalty to rescue a point for Liverpool in the first match of the Andoni Iraola era.
cards.body:
Dominik Szoboszlai's injury-time penalty secured a draw for Liverpool at Newcastle in Andoni Iraola's first match as manager. The result offered relief for the new boss as he began his tenure at Anfield.

However, Liverpool's performance fell short of expectations. The side struggled throughout the match and delivered a below-par display, suggesting Iraola has work ahead to implement his system and improve the team's overall quality of play.

cards.headline: Hull City defeat Manchester United in opening match
cards.teaser: Hull City assistant head coach Dean Holden called the victory over Manchester United beyond anyone's dreams.
cards.body:
Hull City secured a stunning upset victory over Manchester United in their opening match of the season. The promoted hosts exploited a significant weakness in United's defense, scoring twice from set plays within the first 21 minutes—a remarkable achievement given Hull managed only nine set-piece goals throughout their entire Championship campaign last season.

The result represented a disastrous start for Manchester United, who were heavy favorites heading into the match. Opta had rated their chances of victory at nearly 69% before kick-off, making Hull's commanding performance all the more impressive against one of the league's traditional powers.

cards.headline: Marc Guehi excels in midfield role for Manchester City
cards.teaser: Manchester City's Marc Guehi drew praise for his performance in an unfamiliar midfield position against Bournemouth.
cards.body:
Marc Guehi impressed while playing in midfield for Manchester City against Bournemouth, earning acclaim from Match of the Day analyst Joe Hart. The center half was deployed in a different position by manager Enzo Maresca, and the gamble paid off.

Hart discussed Guehi's performance on the program, highlighting how the defender adapted to the midfield role. Maresca's tactical decision to move Guehi from his usual central defensive position proved effective in the match against Bournemouth.

cards.headline: Ollie Watkins omitted from Aston Villa squad amid transfer speculation
cards.teaser: Aston Villa left Ollie Watkins out of their matchday squad against Brighton as speculation links him with a move to Al Hilal.
cards.body:
Ollie Watkins was omitted from Aston Villa's squad for their match against Brighton, with the England striker reportedly considering a move to Saudi Arabian club Al Hilal. Manager Unai Emery did not deny the absence, despite facing a selection crisis with injuries to Brian Madjo and Tammy Abraham. Villa were heavily defeated 4-0 at the Amex, with Emery forced to deploy attacking midfielder Emiliano Buendía as an emergency striker.

Match of the Day analysts discussed whether Watkins wants to leave the club. Gabby Logan suggested it appeared the striker no longer wanted to play for Aston Villa, while Emery deflected questions about the situation, saying it was a matter for Watkins to explain.

hero.headline: Shelley Fabares, Star of The Donna Reed Show and Coach, Dies at 82
hero.body:
Shelley Fabares, the Emmy-nominated actress known for her roles in The Donna Reed Show and the sitcom Coach, has died at age 82. Fabares became a household name playing Mary Stone on The Donna Reed Show, a role she held for five years that launched her career in both television and film.

Fabares appeared in several Elvis Presley films during the 1960s, including Girl Happy, Spinout, and Clambake, becoming part of Hollywood's musical film tradition. Her work opposite Presley helped establish her as a leading actress during that era. She also pursued a music career, releasing recordings that found success on the charts.

In later years, Fabares found renewed television success as Christine Armstrong on the long-running sitcom Coach, which aired from 1989 to 1997. Her performance on the series earned her two Emmy nominations for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Comedy Series. The role introduced her to a new generation of viewers and demonstrated her range as a comedic actress.

Fabares also appeared in other television series throughout her career, including roles on One Day at a Time and various guest appearances on popular shows. She was married to actor Mike Farrell, best known for his role on MAS*H, since 1984. The couple became known for their work together on various humanitarian causes.

Her career spanned more than four decades in entertainment, moving from 1950s wholesome television roles through the evolving landscape of Hollywood into the 1990s. Fabares represented a bridge between different eras of American television, maintaining relevance across multiple generations of viewers.

cards.headline: California Attorney General Cancels Settlement Talks Over Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery Merger
cards.teaser: California's top prosecutor has ended planned negotiations with Paramount over the proposed $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery.
cards.body:
California Attorney General Rob Bonta canceled planned settlement talks with Paramount regarding the state's lawsuit seeking to block the proposed $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery by David Ellison. Bonta accused Paramount of acting in bad faith, according to The New York Times.

Bonta leads a coalition of 12 states challenging the proposed merger. The coalition is asking a court to block the acquisition, which would create one of the largest entertainment conglomerates in the industry. The canceled talks represent an escalation in the legal battle over the deal.

cards.headline: Dutch Broadcaster Withdraws from 2027 Eurovision Over Military Conflict Concerns
cards.teaser: Dutch broadcaster Avrotros pulled out of the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest, citing neutrality concerns.
cards.body:
Avrotros, the Dutch public broadcaster, announced it will not participate in the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest. The broadcaster said the contest can no longer be considered neutral while a participating country remains involved in a large-scale military conflict.

The decision represents a rare political withdrawal from the annual music competition, which typically positions itself as a nonpolitical cultural event. Eurovision has faced pressure in recent years over questions about which countries should be allowed to participate during times of international conflict.

cards.headline: Race Across the World Contestant Jo Gardiner Dies at 61
cards.teaser: Jo Gardiner, who appeared on the television series Race Across the World, died of cancer one year after her son's death.
cards.body:
Jo Gardiner, a contestant from the British television series Race Across the World, has died at age 61 from cancer. Her death occurred one year after her son was killed in a crash.

Gardiner appeared on the travel competition show, which follows teams racing across continents with limited resources and without using air travel. The series is known for highlighting personal stories and relationships between contestants as they navigate demanding journeys.

cards.headline: Brad Pitt Film Heart of the Beast Added to San Sebastián Festival
cards.teaser: The survival thriller starring Brad Pitt and directed by David Ayer will screen out of competition at the Spanish film festival.
cards.body:
Heart of the Beast, starring Brad Pitt and directed by David Ayer, has been added to the San Sebastián Film Festival lineup. The film will screen out of competition in the festival's Official Selection. Both Pitt and Ayer will attend the festival to present the survival thriller.

The film is produced by Paramount Pictures. San Sebastián announced the addition to its lineup, joining other titles competing at one of Europe's major film festivals. The festival takes place annually in Spain and serves as a platform for both international and Spanish cinema.

cards.headline: Venice Film Festival Adds Documentary Naza to Competition Lineup
cards.teaser: The Venice Film Festival added Naza, a documentary from No Other Land directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, to its competition.
cards.body:
The Venice Film Festival has made a last-minute addition to its competition lineup with Naza, a documentary directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor. The filmmaking duo previously collaborated on No Other Land.

The film was shot at night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv and examines Israel's military operations in Gaza. As one of the world's oldest and most prestigious film festivals, Venice competition slots are highly coveted by filmmakers.

cards.headline: Vietnamese Horror Film Lâu Chủ Hòa Heads to North American Theaters
cards.teaser: The Vietnamese found-footage horror film became a breakout hit after its June debut and will open across major theater chains.
cards.body:
Lâu Chủ Hòa: The Deadliest Mansion, a Vietnamese found-footage horror film, will open in North American theaters on September 4. Mockingbird Pictures is placing the title across AMC, Regal, and Cinemark circuits.

Directed by Hồng Trần, the film became Vietnam's first theatrical found-footage horror release. It turned into a breakout hit following its June debut in Vietnam. The North American release represents an expansion of Vietnamese cinema into mainstream theater chains in the United States and Canada.

hero.headline: Trump announces economic campaign against Iran, threatens China sanctions
hero.body:
Trump Extends Iran Ceasefire While Threatening Economic Pressure

President Trump announced an extension of a ceasefire with Iran on Tuesday, pausing military action while demanding Iranian leaders submit a unified peace proposal. The announcement came after weeks of escalating tensions and failed diplomatic efforts between the two nations.

Trump stated on his Truth Social platform that he was extending the ceasefire "until such time as their leaders and representatives can come up with a unified proposal." He credited requests from Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and other officials in his decision to delay military strikes. However, Trump emphasized that the U.S. military would "remain ready and able" and that the blockade on Iranian ports would continue.

The decision marked a sharp reversal from Trump's earlier statements. Hours before announcing the extension, Trump said he "expected to be bombing" and that the military was "raring to go." The administration has threatened to target Iranian power stations and civilian infrastructure in any renewed attacks.

Iran's response has been dismissive. Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, speaker of the Iranian parliament and the regime's lead negotiator, rejected the ceasefire extension. His adviser, Mahdi Mohammadi, wrote on social media that Trump's move was "a ploy to buy time for a surprise strike" and that "the time for Iran to take the initiative has come."

The dispute centers on several key issues. Iran has insisted the U.S. must end its blockade of Iranian ports before negotiations can resume. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that the blockade would continue, stating that within days Iranian oil storage facilities would be full and Iranian wells would shut down.

Trump has also announced plans for what he calls "economic D-Day" against Iran, declaring it "the most crushing economic operation ever taken against any country." Bessent has promised to announce "the toughest sanctions in history" against Iran. The administration has threatened to target any country, business, or banking institution that supports Iran economically.

The ongoing conflict has disrupted global energy markets. Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, a critical shipping lane through which about a fifth of the world's oil and gas passes. The International Energy Agency called the combined effects of this conflict and Russia's war with Ukraine "the biggest crisis in history" for global energy markets. Oil prices have risen above ninety dollars per barrel as a result.

Pakistan has emerged as a key mediator in the dispute. Prime Minister Sharif thanked Trump for the ceasefire extension and pledged to continue efforts toward "a negotiated settlement of the conflict."

The first round of talks in Islamabad ten days earlier ended without agreement on reopening the strait or other key issues. Iran's foreign minister has rejected U.S. threats, calling them "desperate" and insisting that Iran will not negotiate "under the shadow of threats."

cards.headline: Iowa Senate race focuses on cancer rates as contest tightens
cards.teaser: Candidates competing for Iowa's open Senate seat have made the state's high cancer diagnosis rate a central campaign issue.
cards.body:
Democratic state legislator Josh Turek and Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson are competing for Iowa's open Senate seat, left vacant by retiring Sen. Joni Ernst. The contest has become surprisingly competitive this election cycle.

Both candidates have made Iowa's elevated cancer diagnosis rates a focal point of their campaigns, reflecting concerns about public health in the state and seeking to resonate with voters affected by the issue.

cards.headline: Servicemember deployed on USS Lincoln says father detained by ICE
cards.teaser: A sailor aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln reported that his father was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
cards.body:
Joshua Aviles, a sailor aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln deployed in the Middle East, said his father was taken into federal immigration detention. Luis Manuel Aviles Roa, originally from Nicaragua, was arrested by border patrol during a vehicle stop in Key West, Florida, while awaiting green card approval, according to a US Department of Homeland Security spokesperson.

Aviles has been deployed at sea for approximately nine months as part of the military response to tensions with Iran, keeping him separated from his family during this difficult time.

cards.headline: Trump and Michael Cohen reconcile in first public conversation since conviction
cards.teaser: President Trump and his former attorney Michael Cohen spoke publicly for the first time since Cohen testified in the hush money trial.
cards.body:
Trump welcomed Cohen back into his good graces during an interview that aired in full. The conversation covered topics including Trump's proposed ballroom, the economy during his second term, and what Trump called weaponization destroying America.

The interview marks the first time the president and Cohen have spoken publicly since Cohen served as a key witness in the hush money trial that led to Trump's conviction on criminal charges. The remarkably friendly tone of the conversation signaled a shift in their relationship.

cards.headline: Trump defends data center expansion amid state-level opposition
cards.teaser: President Trump said rejecting data centers would be a mistake as the facilities face growing backlash in multiple states.
cards.body:
During an interview with Michael Cohen that aired Sunday, Trump defended data center expansion, calling rejection of the facilities "a mistake." He argued that data centers are building their own power plants rather than relying solely on existing electrical grids.

The president's support comes as data centers face mounting opposition across both Republican and Democratic states over concerns about their substantial energy consumption and environmental impact. Trump also stated the United States maintains a significant lead over China in artificial intelligence development.

cards.headline: Sen. Moreno criticizes discussion of White House aide as misogynistic
cards.teaser: Sen. Bernie Moreno said recent discourse regarding White House aide Natalie Harp has been misogynistic.
cards.body:
The Ohio Republican defended Harp after Democrats and former White House staffers questioned her relationship with President Trump. The Daily Beast reported on letters Harp wrote to Trump in which she expressed allegiance to him.

Moreno characterized the recent discussions about Harp as super misogynistic. Democrats and former administration officials have described Harp's relationship with the president as inappropriate based on the reported correspondence.

cards.headline: Both parties deploy 'radical' label against opponents in midterm campaigns
cards.teaser: Candidates across the political spectrum are using the word radical to describe their opponents as midterm elections approach.
cards.body:
Republicans are labeling Democrats as radical while Democrats are using the same term against Republican candidates. Both parties are making the argument that their opponents represent extreme positions as they prepare for the fall campaign stretch.

The widespread use of the term comes as both political parties face pressure from different factions within their coalitions. Campaigns are deploying the label in an attempt to portray opposing candidates as outside the political mainstream.
